data.content_ref: inline:{"analogy":null,"claim":"The preference smuggles induction back in because any justification for 'acting on' a corroborated theory implicitly assumes the future will resemble the past, violating Popper's strict prohibition.","counterconditions":[{"case":"If 'acting on' can be defined purely as 'selecting for further testing' without expectation of success, the charge fails.","checker_spec":null,"eval":"observation"},{"case":"If Popper can ground the preference in a non-inductive principle like 'verisimilitude' despite technical objections.","checker_spec":null,"eval":"observation"},{"case":"If the preference is merely psychological and not claimed as rational.","checker_spec":null,"eval":"observation"}],"definitions":[],"derivation":[],"formalization_refs":[],"mechanism":"To act on a theory is to expect it to work. If corroboration provides no reason to believe the theory is true or will continue to hold, then preferring it for action is irrational unless one assumes that past survival predicts future performance. This assumption is the definition of induction. Popper's attempt to separate 'corroboration' from 'probability' fails when the stakes involve real-world action, forcing a covert reliance on inductive principles.","premises":[],"schema":"deepreason-reasoning-envelope-v1","scope":{"covers":[],"excludes":[]},"simulation_refs":[],"uncertainties":[]}
